rationale: B wins because it knows where the fact block ends and the pitch begins. Its pricing angle warns that "over 4 million users / most Fortune 500" are company-stated figures and "not used as proof of adoption of this paid seat"; A keeps reaching with "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" and "biggest bet yet." A has useful raw material, but B is the set a founder can act on without accidentally pitching inference as fact.
gaps_in_A: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overclaims the competitive field; the update does not establish a prompt-to-app market, named rivals, or that Make competes with "every" such tool.
"The Adobe deal died. Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" invents magnitude and motive. The facts only say the launch follows the collapsed Adobe acquisition.

"Figma's new $25 AI seat is a bet that Fortune 500 design teams will pay twice" turns existing Figma usage into implied Make adoption and makes "on top of existing plans" sound like literally paying twice.
"what happens to junior front-end developers?" is a viable question, but A leans too hard on "automating a specific, common junior task" without labor data or a Figma statement.
gaps_in_B: "shippable React code" in the headline outruns the supplied fact "working front-end code." B later asks whether engineers would ship it, but the headline should not assume the answer.
"Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died" and "first notable product push" are not established by the update. The fact block says the launch follows the collapse, not that it was first.
B leaves a narrower labor angle unexplored. It rightly rejects vague "future-of-work" mush, but a tightly proofed junior front-end workflow angle could have been usable.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is slightly premature unless real names already exist. Pick the angle, build the target list, then fit-check each journalist.
